title: One surface, many coordinate descriptions
body:
A curved space need not come with one preferred global coordinate grid. We can instead work with overlapping local charts and use smooth conversions to connect their descriptions.
The objects we study belong to the space: scalar measurements, curves, tangent vectors and covectors. Their numerical descriptions depend on the chart, but their meaning does not. The terrain survey below gives one shared example for the six concepts, so that each new mathematical object has a practical role.
statement: Compatible local charts describe one surface; vectors and covectors describe motion and scalar readouts.

title: The kame-and-kettle survey
body:
A group of soil scientists wants to compare temperature, grass growth and curvature on a strongly undulating kame-and-kettle landscape. They treat the ground itself as a two-dimensional surface, rather than replacing it by a horizontal map.
Each scientist takes a small overlapping patch and places a rigid board tangent to the ground at a reference point. The board has a straight two-dimensional grid, but its scale, orientation and even the angle between its axes can differ from the neighbours' grids. Its position and orientation can be reproduced when measurements are revisited.
Nearby ground points receive board coordinates through a smooth one-to-one projection. The patch must be small enough for the projection and its inverse to remain well behaved. Thus a flat board supplies convenient labels; it does not make the ground flat or guarantee that board distances equal surface distances.
Neighbouring scientists compare pegs in their overlaps and agree smooth conversions between their coordinate pairs. They record temperature \(T\), a surface grass-growth direction and length \(G\), and an intrinsic curvature estimate \(K\) at pegged points. A mobile probe also follows a route through several patches.
At the club hut, a mathematician helps them combine the records. Despite their incompatible-looking spreadsheets, the scientists have described one ground surface and one set of physical measurements.
statement: Overlapping board grids describe one curved ground surface and the same measurements.

title: The mathematician's dictionary
body:
The complete ground surface is a \cref{manifold}{math.manifold.definition} \(M\). One scientist's patch and board labels form a \cref{coordinate chart}{math.coordinate_chart.definition} \((U_i,x_i)\), while the agreed rule on an overlap is a coordinate transformation.
The mobile probe follows a parametrised surface curve \(\gamma(t)\). Including time turns that route into a spacetime history, or worldline. Its instantaneous surface velocity and the grass-growth direction are tangent vectors: both describe motion or direction at a particular ground point.
Temperature and the measured curvature estimate are scalar fields, \(T:M\rightarrow\mathbb R\) and \(K:M\rightarrow\mathbb R\). Their differentials \(dT\) and \(dK\) are covector fields. Given a tangent direction, each differential reads the instantaneous change of its scalar along that direction. This is how the measurements lead naturally from points and coordinates to vectors and covectors.
statement: The terrain survey gives concrete meanings to manifolds, charts, curves, vectors and covectors.

title: One coordinate-independent measurement
body:
Let the probe follow a surface curve \(\gamma(t)\), with time \(t\) in seconds, through a smooth time-independent temperature field \(T\). The \cref{directional-derivative interpretation}{math.tangent_space.directional_derivative} gives the temperature rate along its tangent velocity. The \cref{dual-basis rule}{math.cotangent_space.basis} expresses that readout as a component sum:
\[\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dt}T(\gamma(t))
 &=dT_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\dot\gamma(t)\bigr)\\
 &=\left.\frac{\partial T}{\partial x^i}\right|_{\gamma(t)}
   \frac{dx^i}{dt}.
\end{aligned}\]
Here \(i=1,2\) is summed in a board chart. The vector supplies the probe's coordinate rates; the covector supplies the temperature derivatives. Under a chart change these components acquire inverse factors, so they compensate in the pairing. Both scientists therefore predict the same physical temperature rate.
Similarly, \(dT(G)\) tests whether surface grass growth points locally towards warmer ground, colder ground or along an isotherm. Asking which direction gives the greatest change at a fixed physical speed needs an additional measuring rule: a metric.
statement: The scalar temperature rate is the same whichever board coordinates describe the motion.

title: Looking ahead: metric and curvature
body:
Coordinates label the ground, but they do not alone determine lengths, angles, geodesics or curvature. Those require a metric, introduced later. For the present survey, we can simply treat the scientists' curvature estimate as a measured scalar \(K(p)\), alongside temperature.
For a glimpse of the further geometry, consider a small geodesic circle centred at \(p\), with surface radius \(r\) and circumference \(C(r)\). On a flat plane its circumference would be \(2\pi r\). The small departure from that ratio carries information about Gaussian curvature:
\[K(p)\simeq\frac{6}{r^2}\left(1-\frac{C(r)}{2\pi r}\right).\]
A careful point estimate uses several radii and extrapolates towards \(r=0\), rather than treating one finite circle as exact. This is a preview of what a metric lets us measure; the core coordinate, vector and covector arguments in this module do not require a curvature calculation.
statement: Lengths and curvature require a metric; coordinates alone supply neither.

title: From local readouts to tensor components
body:
This module builds the tensor tools needed for GR. Start with vectors, covectors and their natural pairing from MATHS-1. Tensors extend that readout idea to several inputs; a tensor field supplies such an object at each point.
We first distinguish type and order, then calculate two-input measurements and contractions. The transformation law combines two ingredients: coordinate Jacobians tell us how bases change, and multilinearity tells us how one change in each input affects the readout. Index notation keeps track of the resulting products and sums.
The two-dimensional terrain remains a useful example, while GR applies the same constructions at four-dimensional spacetime events. Metrics, stress-energy and curvature motivate their use. Abstract-index notation is optional supporting detail; covariant differentiation, connections and curvature calculations are developed later in GR, rather than assumed here.
statement: Tensor slots, contractions and component transformations provide the working language for GR.
